intro.why: Every deep network is built from these neurons; the perceptron's update rule foreshadows gradient descent, and its failure on XOR is the reason for hidden layers (Module 5).

sections.title: How do humans learn? The brain
sections.body: Questions for the module: what is an artificial neuron, how is it related to a biological neuron, how are neurons interconnected, how do they learn? Humans learn, solve problems, recognise patterns and create, largely through association (associationism). Observations: the brain is a mass of interconnected neurons; about $10^{10}$ neurons; about $10^{4\text{–}5}$ connections per neuron; neuron switching time about 0.001 s; scene recognition about 1 s. So only ~100 sequential inference steps are possible: the brain must rely on a lot of parallel computation.

sections.title: Biological neuron structure
sections.body:
• Dendrites: receive signals from other neurons.
  • Cell body (soma): processes incoming signals.
  • Axon: transmits the output signal.
  • Synapses: connection points between neurons.

Mapping to the artificial neuron: dendrites ↔ inputs, synaptic strengths ↔ weights, soma ↔ summation + activation, axon ↔ output.

sections.title: What is an artificial neuron?
sections.plain: A processing element; knowledge stored as parameters.
sections.body: Definition: an artificial neuron is a processing element inspired by how the brain works. Like a biological neuron it performs some computation and is interconnected with other neurons; as in the brain, the interconnections store the knowledge it learns, as parameters. Neuron $N$ receives $x_1..x_n$ and a constant 1 with weight $b$; it performs a weighted sum, each weight $w_i$ expressing the importance of feature $x_i$, and generates one numerical output $\hat y$.

sections.title: Mathematical computation
sections.body:
$$z=\sum_{i=1}^nw_ix_i+b\qquad(1)\qquad\qquad \hat y=f\Big(\sum_{i=1}^nw_ix_i+b\Big)\qquad(2)$$

Sum of weights times features, then apply the activation $f$. In vector form $z=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b$. With $f$ = step or sign, the neuron is a linear threshold unit; with $f=\sigma$ (sigmoid) it is logistic regression; with $f$ = identity, linear regression (Modules 3–4).

sections.title: Biological vs artificial neurons
sections.body:
Biological neuronArtificial neuron
Complex biochemical processesSimple mathematical model
Analog signal processingDigital computation
Adaptive synaptic strengthsAdjustable weights
Parallel processingParallel computation possible
Learning through experienceLearning through algorithms
Fault tolerantDeterministic behaviour

Key insight: artificial neurons are simplified mathematical abstractions that capture the essential computational properties of biological neurons.

sections.title: What are artificial neural networks?
sections.plain: Interconnected neurons in input, hidden and output layers.
sections.body: A neural network is a computational model inspired by the brain: interconnected neurons process information; interconnections can be forward, recursive or self-loops; it learns patterns from data through training and is capable of approximating complex functions. The figure shows an input layer, several hidden layers and an output layer, fully connected between consecutive layers. A layer computes $\mathbf h^{(l)}=f(W^{(l)}\mathbf h^{(l-1)}+\mathbf b^{(l)})$.

sections.title: Properties of ANNs
sections.plain: Many neurons, weighted links, parallel, self-tuning.
sections.body:
• Many neurons.
  • Many weighted interconnections among neurons.
  • Highly parallel, distributed processing.
  • Tuning parameters (weights) automatically.

sections.title: When to consider ANNs
sections.plain: High-dimensional, noisy inputs; unknown target; explainability unimportant.
sections.body:
• Input is high-dimensional discrete or real-valued (e.g. raw sensor input).
  • Possibly noisy data with errors.
  • Output is discrete, real-valued or a vector of values.
  • The form of the target function is unknown.
  • Human readability (explainability) of the result is unimportant.
  • Examples: speech recognition, image classification, financial prediction.

sections.title: Connectionist machines
sections.body: A network of processing elements (artificial neurons) interconnected to form a network; connections can be forward, recursive or self-loop; all world knowledge is stored in the connections between elements. Neural networks are connectionist machines.

sections.title: Connectionism principles
sections.plain: Simple units, weights as knowledge, learning changes weights, parallelism.
sections.body:
• Intelligence emerges from simple processing neurons.
  • Knowledge is stored in connection weights.
  • Learning modifies connection strengths.
  • Parallel distributed processing.

Historical note: Hebb's rule (1949), "cells that fire together wire together", $\Delta w_{ij}=\eta\,x_ix_j$, was an early learning principle of this kind; the perceptron rule adds error correction.

sections.title: The perceptron
sections.body:
The perceptron is the simplest form of artificial neuron, introduced by Rosenblatt in 1958. With inputs $x_1,x_2,x_3$, weights $w_1,w_2,w_3$ and bias $b$:

$$\hat y=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\sum_{i=1}^nw_ix_i+b\ge0\\-1&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Decision boundary: the hyperplane $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+b=0$, with $\mathbf w$ normal to it.

sections.title: Representing logic gates
sections.body: Power of the perceptron: any linear decision can be represented by a Boolean equation; the quest is to represent such decisions with a perceptron, so we test whether each logic gate can be represented. Output conventions: Rosenblatt's classical perceptron uses $\{-1,+1\}$; modern implementations and logic gates often use $\{0,1\}$; both are valid, and the choice affects only the bias/threshold calculation. The numerical examples use $\{0,1\}$.

sections.title: Perceptron for AND
sections.body:
Truth table: AB = 1 only for (1, 1). With $\hat y=w_0x_0+w_1x_1+w_2x_2$, $x_0=1$, find $w_0,w_1,w_2$ satisfying:

$$\begin{array}{cc|c|l}x_1&x_2&t&h\\\hline0&0&0&w_0<0\\0&1&0&w_0+w_2<0\\1&0&0&w_0+w_1<0\\1&1&1&w_0+w_1+w_2\ge0\end{array}$$

One solution: $w_0=-1$, $w_1=0.75$, $w_2=0.75$: $h=-1,-0.25,-0.25,0.5$. Geometrically the line $0.75x_1+0.75x_2=1$ separates (1, 1) from the other three corners. Any $w_1,w_2>0$ with $w_1<-w_0$, $w_2<-w_0$, $w_1+w_2\ge-w_0$ works (our learning run found $w=(-3,2,1)$).

sections.title: Perceptron for OR
sections.body: A + B = 0 only for (0, 0). Inequalities: $w_0<0$; $w_0+w_2\ge0$; $w_0+w_1\ge0$; $w_0+w_1+w_2\ge0$. One solution: $w_0=-1$, $w_1=2$, $w_2=2$: $h=-1,1,1,3$. Geometrically the line $2x_1+2x_2=1$ separates (0, 0) from the rest.

sections.title: Perceptron learning algorithm
sections.plain: Update only on mistakes: w ← w + η(t − ŷ)x.
sections.body:
Goal: find weights that correctly classify the training pairs $(x,t)$.

1. initialise learning rate η (e.g. 0.1)
2. initialise weights w_i randomly (or to 0)
3. for each training example (x, t):
      ŷ ← sign(Σ_i w_i x_i + b)          // step for {0,1} outputs
      if ŷ ≠ t:
         w_i ← w_i + η (t − ŷ) x_i        for all i
         b   ← b   + η (t − ŷ)
4. repeat 3 until convergence (an epoch with no mistakes) or max iterations

Convergence theorem: if the data are linearly separable, the perceptron algorithm converges in a finite number of steps. (Novikoff, 1962: if $\|\mathbf x\|\le R$ and some unit $\mathbf w^*$ separates the data with margin $\gamma$, the number of mistakes is at most $(R/\gamma)^2$, independent of η and of the number of examples.) The rule is stochastic gradient descent on the perceptron criterion $-\sum_{\text{mistakes}}t\,\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$ (with $t\in\{-1,+1\}$).

sections.title: The XOR problem
sections.body: Truth table: $x_1\oplus x_2=0,1,1,0$ for (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1). Plotted on the unit square, the 1s sit at (0, 1) and (1, 0), the 0s at (0, 0) and (1, 1). XOR is not linearly separable; a single perceptron cannot solve it.

sections.title: Why a single perceptron fails on XOR
sections.body: Any line $w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b=0$ fails. Proof by inequalities: we would need $b<0$ (0,0), $w_2+b\ge0$ (0,1), $w_1+b\ge0$ (1,0), $w_1+w_2+b<0$ (1,1). Adding the middle two gives $w_1+w_2+2b\ge0$, i.e. $w_1+w_2+b\ge-b>0$, contradicting the last. Solution: multiple layers (multilayer perceptron), e.g. $h_1=\text{OR}(x_1,x_2)$, $h_2=\text{NAND}(x_1,x_2)$, $\hat y=\text{AND}(h_1,h_2)$. Minsky & Papert's 1969 analysis of such limits contributed to the first "AI winter".

sections.title: Linearly separable data
sections.body: Two sets of points in $n$-dimensional space are linearly separable if an $(n-1)$-dimensional hyperplane separates them. In 2-D, a straight line separates all class +1 examples from all class −1 examples. If so, infinitely many such lines exist; the perceptron returns one of them (not necessarily the maximum-margin one; compare SVMs).

sections.title: Perceptron for linearly separable data
sections.plain: Data, model, objective, algorithm; vector form ŷ = step(wᵀx̃).
sections.body:
Framing: data: truth tables or example sets; model: perceptron, inputs $x$ (features/columns), target $t$ (label); objective: deviation between target $t$ and output $\hat y$; learning algorithm: perceptron learning. Challenge: learn the $n+1$ parameters $w_0,\dots,w_n$. Vector form:

$$\tilde{\mathbf x}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\x_1\\\vdots\\x_n\end{bmatrix},\ \mathbf w=\begin{bmatrix}w_0\\w_1\\\vdots\\w_n\end{bmatrix},\qquad h=w_0+w_1x_1+\dots+w_nx_n=\mathbf w^T\tilde{\mathbf x},\qquad \hat y=\begin{cases}1&h\ge0\\0&h<0\end{cases}$$

sections.title: Key concepts
sections.plain: Neuron, perceptron, learning rule, XOR limit.
sections.body:
• Neural network: computational model inspired by biological neurons that processes information through interconnected units.
  • Perceptron: single-layer linear classifier $\hat y=\text{sign}(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x)$; learning rule $w_i^{(new)}=w_i^{(old)}+\eta(t-\hat y)x_i$; converges for linearly separable data.
  • Limitations: cannot solve XOR and other non-linearly separable problems; solution: multi-layer networks with non-linear activation functions.
  • These concepts form the foundation of deep learning architectures.

sections.title: Comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
PerceptronLogistic regressionLinear SVM
OutputHard labelProbabilitySigned score
UpdateOnly on mistakesEvery example (gradient)Hinge-loss gradient
Solution on separable dataAny separatorWeights grow unboundedly without regularisationMaximum-margin separator
Non-separable dataNever convergesConverges (convex)Converges (soft margin)
  • "The learning rate changes whether the perceptron converges." With zero initial weights, η only rescales w; the mistake sequence is identical.
  • "The perceptron minimises misclassification error." It minimises the perceptron criterion; with non-separable data it oscillates (the pocket algorithm keeps the best weights seen).
  • "Deep networks are just stacked perceptrons." They use differentiable activations (sigmoid, ReLU) so gradients can flow; step functions have zero gradient almost everywhere.

code.title: Perceptron by hand: AND, OR, the NOT trace and XOR
code.explain: Checks the AND and OR weights, reproduces the NOT-gate learning trace exactly, and shows that the rule converges for AND and OR but never for XOR.
mistakes: Using h > 0 instead of h ≥ 0: the NOT trace then behaves differently at h = 0.
code.notes: Integer learning rate η = 1 avoids floating-point ties at h = 0.

code.title: scikit-learn Perceptron and an MLP for XOR
code.explain: Perceptron reaches 100% on separable blobs; on XOR it stays at 50%; a one-hidden-layer MLP solves XOR.
mistakes: Expecting the perceptron to return a maximum-margin boundary.
code.notes: Hidden layers with non-linear activations are developed in DNN Module 5.
code.code:
# scikit-learn Perceptron on separable data, and why XOR needs a hidden layer
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Perceptron
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs
X, y = make_blobs(200, centers=[[-2, -2], [2, 2]], cluster_std=1.0, random_state=0)
p = Perceptron(eta0=0.1, max_iter=1000, random_state=0).fit(X, y)
print("separable blobs: accuracy", p.score(X, y), "epochs", p.n_iter_, "w", np.round(p.coef_[0], 2), "b", np.round(p.intercept_, 2))
Xx = np.array([[0, 0], [0, 1], [1, 0], [1, 1]]); yx = np.array([0, 1, 1, 0])
print("XOR with a perceptron: accuracy", Perceptron(max_iter=1000, random_state=0).fit(Xx, yx).score(Xx, yx))
m = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(4,), activation="tanh", solver="lbfgs", random_state=1, max_iter=2000).fit(Xx, yx)
print("XOR with one hidden layer of 4 tanh units: accuracy", m.score(Xx, yx), " predictions", m.predict(Xx))
